stem: A 34-year-old photojournalist returns to the United States 9 days after completing a 3-week assignment in rural sub-Saharan Africa. He did not take pharmacological malaria chemoprophylaxis. He presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of cyclical high fevers, rigors, drenching sweats, severe headache, nausea, and dark urine. On presentation, he is disoriented to time and place. Vital signs are: temperature 39.8 C, pulse 124/min, blood pressure 88/54 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 24/min. Physical examination demonstrates scleral icterus, dry oral mucous membranes, and splenomegaly; no nuchal rigidity or focal neurological deficits are present. Laboratory testing demonstrates: hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, platelet count 36,000/mm3, total bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL (direct 1.1 mg/dL), serum creatinine 2.6 mg/dL, and venous lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Giemsa-stained peripheral blood thin and thick smears demonstrate intraerythrocytic ring-form trophozoites with multiple rings per red blood cell and banana-shaped gametocytes, with a calculated Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia of 12%. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient severe infection, and what mandatory safety testing is required before administering primaquine in patients with relapsing malarial species?

options.text: Oral chloroquine phosphate monotherapy; screening for sickle cell trait is mandatory prior to primaquine administration
options.explanation: P. falciparum has widespread chloroquine resistance, and oral medications cannot treat severe malaria with shock; G6PD (not sickle trait) is tested.

options.text: Intravenous quinidine gluconate plus clindamycin; serum cholinesterase activity testing is mandatory prior to primaquine administration
options.explanation: IV artesunate has replaced quinidine due to lower mortality and lack of cardiotoxicity; G6PD (not cholinesterase) must be screened.

options.text: Intravenous artesunate is the first-line therapy of choice; quantitative glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity testing is mandatory prior to primaquine administration
options.explanation: This patient presents with SEVERE, LIFE-THREATENING PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM MALARIA. High-yield concepts tested on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) SEVERE MALARIA DEFINITION: Severe malaria is diagnosed when Plasmodium infection is complicated by any of the following clinical or laboratory features: (a) Impaired consciousness, delirium, or cerebral malaria; (b) High parasitemia (> 5% to 10% of circulating red blood cells infected); (c) Severe normocytic anemia (hemoglobin < 7 g/dL); (d) Acute kidney injury (creatinine > 3 mg/dL); (e) Pulmonary edema or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); (f) Circulatory collapse/hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mm Hg); (g) Acidosis (plasma bicarbonate < 15 mEq/L or lactate > 4 mmol/L); or (h) Spontaneous macroscopic bleeding or disseminated intravascular coagulation. topic: Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis Diagnosis Probe-to-Bone and Bone Biopsy
stem: A 61-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by dense distal sensory polyneuropathy presents with a non-healing ulcer on the plantar surface of his right first metatarsal head. He has noticed yellowish drainage on his sock for the past 4 weeks but feels no pain or systemic symptoms. Physical examination reveals an alert, afebrile man with normal vital signs. Examination of the right plantar foot demonstrates a 2.4-cm x 1.8-cm painless, punched-out ulceration with callous borders and purulent exudate. Distal peripheral pulses are 1+ bilaterally with delayed capillary refill. During bedside evaluation, the physician gently inserts a sterile, blunt metallic probe into the base of the ulcer; the probe advances deeply and stops against a hard, gritty, rigid surface, eliciting a metallic click (positive probe-to-bone test). Plain radiographs of the right foot show soft tissue swelling around the first metatarsal head without definitive cortical erosion, periosteal reaction, or osteolysis. Laboratory testing reveals: WBC 8,600/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 88 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein (CRP) 42 mg/L. Which of the following represents the most appropriate sequence of diagnostic steps to confirm the diagnosis and guide definitive antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Swab the superficial purulent discharge from the ulcer base for bacterial cultures and initiate empiric oral cephalexin
options.explanation: Superficial swabs reflect surface colonizers, not true pathogens invading bone; cephalexin monotherapy misses Gram-negatives and MRSA.

options.text: Obtain a repeat plain radiograph in 6 months and withhold further testing because initial X-rays showed no osteolysis
options.explanation: Waiting 6 months allows osteomyelitis to progress to extensive gangrene, tissue necrosis, and proximal leg amputation.

options.text: Perform a technetium-99m bone scan with gallium-67 imaging as the definitive anatomical test of choice
options.explanation: Triple-phase bone scans cannot distinguish between osteomyelitis, Charcot neuroarthropathy, and soft tissue inflammation; MRI is superior.

options.text: Perform magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the foot to evaluate for bone marrow edema and obtain an operative or percutaneous bone biopsy for culture and histopathology
options.explanation: This patient presents with a chronic, non-healing neuropathic plantar foot ulcer with high clinical suspicion for DIABETIC FOOT OSTEOMYELITIS. Master the diagnostic algorithm on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) BEDSIDE SCREENING — THE PROBE-TO-BONE TEST: In patients with a deep, non-healing diabetic ulcer (> 2 cm2 or lasting > 2 weeks), palpating hard, gritty bone with a sterile, blunt metallic probe has a sensitivity of ~87% and a positive predictive value approaching 90% in high-risk populations. A positive probe-to-bone test strongly suggests underlying osteomyelitis. (2) IMAGING EVALUATION: Initial imaging is plain radiographs (X-rays). However, conventional X-rays have poor sensitivity in early or subacute osteomyelitis, appearing completely normal for the first 10 to 14 days because radiographic osteolysis and periosteal reaction require 30% to 50% loss of trabecular bone mineralization. When clinical suspicion remains high (such as an ESR > 70 mm/hr or positive probe-to-bone) despite normal plain films, the DEFINITIVE IMAGING MODALITY OF CHOICE IS MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING (MRI) OF THE FOOT. MRI exhibits >90% sensitivity and specificity, accurately detecting bone marrow edema (hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2/STIR), cortical breach, sinus tracts, and deep fascial space abscesses. (3) MICROBIOLOGICAL GOLD STANDARD — BONE BIOPSY: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis is frequently polymicrobial (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas, and anaerobes). The undisputed GOLD STANDARD for definitive diagnosis and targeted antibiotic selection is PERCUTANEOUS OR OPERATIVE BONE BIOPSY FOR HISTOPATHOLOGY AND MICROBIOLOGICAL CULTURE, obtained through uninfected skin. (4) INADEQUACY OF SUPERFICIAL SWABS: Taking a superficial swab of the ulcer base or purulent drainage is CONTRAINDICATED TO GUIDE ANTIMICROBIAL THERAPY. Superficial swabs merely isolate colonizing commensal surface flora (such as coagulase-negative staphylococci or colonizing diphtheroids) and correlate poorly with the true pathogens invading deep bone, leading to inappropriate antibiotic selection and progressive limb-threatening bone necrosis.

options.text: Perform immediate bedside surgical debridement followed by 6 weeks of empiric oral ciprofloxacin without obtaining cultures
options.explanation: Ciprofloxacin monotherapy provides inadequate Gram-positive coverage; antibiotic therapy must be tailored to definitive bone biopsy cultures.

stem: A 74-year-old man residing in a skilled nursing facility is evaluated for acute-onset fever, shivering chills, and new-onset confusion that developed over the past 12 hours. He has a history of severe benign prostatic hyperplasia and ischemic stroke with residual dense hemiplegia; an indwelling transurethral Foley catheter was placed 3 weeks ago for chronic urinary retention and has remained continuously in place. On physical examination, he is disoriented and lethargic. Vital signs are: temperature 38.8 C, pulse 108/min, blood pressure 102/64 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20/min. Abdominal examination demonstrates suprapubic tenderness to deep palpation without guarding or rebound tenderness; costovertebral angles are non-tender. The indwelling catheter contains cloudy, dark amber urine with visible sedimentary debris. The nursing staff prepares to collect a urine sample for analysis and culture. The patient continues to require bladder catheterization due to severe urethral obstruction. Which of the following is the most appropriate management step regarding catheter care and diagnostic urine collection for this patient?

options.text: Aspirate urine immediately from the sampling port of the existing 3-week-old catheter to avoid the trauma of catheter replacement
options.explanation: Aspirating from an old catheter samples biofilm organisms; guidelines mandate catheter replacement before culture collection if in place >= 2 weeks.

options.text: Irrigate the existing catheter lumen with 50 mL of continuous neomycin-polymyxin bladder wash for 48 hours before culturing
options.explanation: Antimicrobial bladder irrigations do not eradicate catheter biofilms and are strongly discouraged due to risk of selecting resistant organisms.

options.text: Clamp the catheter drainage tube for 4 hours, disconnect the collection bag, and collect drainage directly from the tubing
options.explanation: Disconnecting the closed drainage system breaks sterile integrity, introducing exogenous hospital pathogens and increasing bacteremia risk.

options.text: Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for 7 days, and replace the catheter only if urine cultures show no bacterial growth
options.explanation: Bacteria protected within the biofilm cannot be eradicated by systemic antibiotics alone; the colonized foreign body must be exchanged.

options.text: Remove the existing indwelling catheter, insert a new sterile Foley catheter, and obtain the urine culture specimen directly from the freshly placed catheter prior to initiating targeted antibiotics
options.explanation: This patient presents with a symptomatic CATHETER-ASSOCIATED URINARY TRACT INFECTION (CAUTI), characterized by fever, rigors, suprapubic tenderness, delirium, and cloudy urine in the presence of an indwelling urethral catheter. Master the evidence-based CAUTI management protocol established by the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA): (1) PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF CATHETER BIOFILMS: Within days of indwelling urinary catheterization, bacteria adhere to the synthetic silicone or latex surfaces, producing an extracellular polymeric substance matrix that forms a dense, complex MICROBIAL BIOFILM. Organisms embedded within biofilms enter a slow-growing stationary phase that renders them highly resistant to antimicrobial penetration and host immune defenses. Over 2 to 3 weeks, virtually all indwelling catheters become colonized with polymicrobial biofilms (often harboring Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, Proteus, or Candida). (2) THE DIAGNOSTIC PITFALL OF SAMPLING OLD CATHETERS: Obtaining a urine specimen from an indwelling catheter that has been in place for >= 2 weeks is a major clinical diagnostic pitfall. The aspirated urine samples organisms sloughed from the intraluminal biofilm rather than the true pathogen driving acute parenchymal bladder or renal infection. This results in misleading culture results, unnecessary broad-spectrum antimicrobial overuse, and failure to treat the real underlying pathogen. (3) IDSA GUIDELINE RECOMMENDATIONS: (a) If the catheter is no longer strictly medically indicated, it should be permanently discontinued. (b) IF THE INDWELLING CATHETER HAS BEEN IN PLACE FOR >= 2 WEEKS AND REMAINS MEDICALLY NECESSARY (such as chronic anatomic outlet obstruction in this patient), THE OLD CATHETER MUST BE REMOVED AND REPLACED WITH A NEW STERILE CATHETER. (c) The diagnostic urine culture specimen must then be obtained from the FRESHLY PLACED CATHETER (or midstream specimen if the catheter is removed). (d) Replacing the colonized catheter prior to antibiotic therapy significantly accelerates clinical resolution, decreases the duration of fever, and reduces CAUTI relapse rates.

stem: A 64-year-old man who was admitted to the intensive care unit 6 days ago for severe acute pancreatitis complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is maintained on mechanical ventilation. Two days ago, he completed a 5-day course of intravenous ciprofloxacin for a suspected biliary tract infection. Over the past 12 hours, his respiratory status has deteriorated: the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) requirement has increased from 40% to 75%, and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) has been escalated from 8 to 14 cm H2O. Physical examination reveals an intubated, sedated man with a temperature of 39.1 C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg, and coarse rhonchi throughout the right hemithorax. Copious thick, purulent, yellowish secretions are suctioned from the endotracheal tube. A portable chest radiograph reveals a new, dense consolidation in the right middle and lower lobes that was not present on admission films. Laboratory testing demonstrates: WBC 21,400/mm3 (88% neutrophils, 8% bands) and PaO2/FiO2 ratio 140 mm Hg. An endotracheal aspirate is obtained for Gram stain and quantitative culture. Which of the following represents the most appropriate, guideline-adherent empiric antimicrobial regimen for this patient?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin plus intravenous cefepime (or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus intravenous amikacin (or levofloxacin)
options.explanation: This patient presents with definitive VENTILATOR-ASSOCIATED PNEUMONIA (VAP) occurring in a high-risk intensive care unit setting. Master the IDSA/ATS guidelines on VAP diagnosis and empiric therapy: (1) DEFINITION: VAP is defined as hospital-acquired pneumonia developing >= 48 hours after endotracheal intubation. The diagnosis requires a new or worsening radiographic pulmonary infiltrate combined with clinical evidence of infection: fever > 38 C, purulent endotracheal secretions, leukocytosis, and deteriorating oxygenation (declining PaO2/FiO2 ratio). (2) MULTIDRUG-RESISTANT (MDR) RISK FACTORS: This patient possesses multiple major risk factors for multidrug-resistant pathogens: (a) Hospitalization for >= 5 days (day 6 of admission); (b) Receipt of prior intravenous antibiotics within the past 90 days (ciprofloxacin 2 days ago); (c) Preceding ARDS; and (d) Septic shock / hemodynamic instability requiring high ventilator settings. (3) GUIDELINE-MANDATED EMPIRIC ANTIMICROBIAL REGIMEN: In patients with VAP who have risk factors for antimicrobial resistance or are in ICUs with high rates of resistance, IDSA/ATS guidelines strictly mandate a THREE-DRUG EMPIRIC REGIMEN: (a) ONE AGENT ACTIVE AGAINST MRSA: Vancomycin (targeting a trough of 15-20 mcg/mL or AUC/MIC 400-600) OR Linezolid (600 mg IV every 12 hours). (b) TWO DIVERSE ANTIPSEUDOMONAL AGENTS FROM DIFFERENT PHARMACOLOGICAL CLASSES: To ensure adequate bactericidal coverage against resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) Enterobacteriaceae: - Agent 1: An antipseudomonal beta-lactam (such as CEFEPIME, PIPERACILLIN-TAZOBACTAM, or MEROPENEM); PLUS - Agent 2: A non-beta-lactam antipseudomonal agent: either an antipseudomonal aminoglycoside (AMIKACIN, tobramycin, or gentamicin) OR an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin; though amikacin is preferred here due to prior recent fluoroquinolone exposure). (4) Once high-quality endotracheal quantitative cultures (>= 10^6 CFU/mL for aspirate, >= 10^4 CFU/mL for bronchoalveolar lavage) and sensitivities return at 48 to 72 hours, antimicrobial therapy is promptly de-escalated to a single targeted agent.

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily
options.explanation: Ceftriaxone and azithromycin treat community-acquired pneumonia; they have zero activity against MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy, withholding MRSA coverage until sputum cultures confirm Gram-positive cocci
options.explanation: In high-risk VAP, omitting MRSA coverage and dual gram-negative coverage leads to unacceptably high early mortality from resistant organisms.

options.text: Intravenous linezolid monotherapy combined with aerosolized colistin
options.explanation: Linezolid monotherapy provides zero systemic coverage against Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter; systemic IV antipseudomonals are mandatory.

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus high-dose intravenous dexamethasone
options.explanation: TMP-SMX is not empiric therapy for VAP, and corticosteroids increase secondary ICU infections without improving VAP survival.

Monotherapy or single gram-negative coverage is inadequate in high-risk VAP!

topic: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in Pregnancy Screening and Antimicrobial Regimens
stem: A 26-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 2 para 1, presents for a routine prenatal visit at 14 weeks gestation. She is completely asymptomatic and reports feeling well with normal fetal movements. She specifically denies dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, flank pain, fever, chills, or vaginal discharge. Her past medical history is unremarkable, and her first pregnancy resulted in an uncomplicated full-term vaginal delivery. Physical examination reveals an alert, afebrile woman with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with a gravid uterus consistent with 14 weeks size; costovertebral angles are non-tender bilaterally. A clean-catch midstream urine culture obtained at her first visit 5 days ago demonstrates growth of Escherichia coli with a colony count of > 100,000 CFU/mL (> 10^5 CFU/mL), susceptible to ampicillin, cephalexin, nitrofurantoin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Urinalysis reveals 10-15 WBCs/hpf and negative nitrites. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?

options.text: Withhold antimicrobial therapy and reassure the patient that treatment is indicated only if she develops dysuria, fever, or flank pain
options.explanation: Withholding therapy in pregnancy leads to acute pyelonephritis in up to 40% of cases, triggering preterm labor and fetal loss.

options.text: Prescribe oral ciprofloxacin 250 mg twice daily for 3 days and repeat screening only if symptoms develop in the third trimester
options.explanation: Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal chondrotoxicity, and follow-up test-of-cure cultures are mandatory.

options.text: Initiate a 5-to-7 day course of oral cephalexin (or amoxicillin-clavulanate) and obtain a repeat urine culture (test-of-cure) 1 to 2 weeks after completing therapy
options.explanation: This pregnant woman presents with documented ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA IN PREGNANCY. Key clinical and management principles on USMLE Step 2 CK: (1) DEFINITION AND SCREENING: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is defined as the isolation of a single bacterial species in quantitative counts >= 10^5 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL in a clean-catch midstream voided urine specimen in a patient with zero symptoms of urinary tract infection. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) mandate universal screening with a quantitative urine culture for ALL pregnant women at their first prenatal visit or at 12 to 16 weeks gestation. (2) CONTRAST WITH NON-PREGNANT ADULTS: In non-pregnant adults, elderly patients, diabetics, and individuals with spinal cord injuries, asymptomatic bacteriuria is benign and MUST NOT BE TREATED; antibiotic administration in non-pregnant patients does not prevent infections and drives multidrug resistance. IN PREGNANCY, HOWEVER, ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA MUST ALWAYS BE TREATED! (3) RATIONALE: Progesterone-induced ureteral smooth muscle dilation, decreased peristalsis, and mechanical compression by the gravid uterus lead to marked urinary stasis and vesicoureteral reflux. In pregnant women, untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria has a 30% to 40% risk of progressing to acute pyelonephritis, which is strongly associated with severe maternal sepsis, ARDS, preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), preterm labor, low birth weight, and perinatal mortality. (4) SAFE ANTIMICROBIAL CHOICES: First-line safe oral options include: ORAL CEPHALEXIN (500 mg every 6 hours for 5 to 7 days), AMOXICILLIN-CLAVULANATE, NITROFURANTOIN (avoid during the first trimester if alternatives exist, and avoid at term >37 weeks due to risk of neonatal hemolytic anemia/hyperbilirubinemia), or a single 3 g dose of ORAL FOSFOMYCIN. Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated (fetal cartilage toxicity). (5) MANDATORY POST-TREATMENT TEST-OF-CURE: Because bacterial persistence and recurrence are common (~30%), guidelines dictate that A REPEAT URINE CULTURE (TEST-OF-CURE) MUST BE OBTAINED 1 TO 2 WEEKS AFTER COMPLETION OF THERAPY to verify complete bacterial clearance. Periodic surveillance urine cultures are continued throughout pregnancy.

options.text: Prescribe single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g followed by daily oral phenazopyridine until delivery
options.explanation: Parenteral ceftriaxone is reserved for inpatient pyelonephritis; phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that does not treat bacteria.

options.text: Schedule immediate cystoscopy to evaluate for anatomical bladder trabeculation or urethral diverticula
options.explanation: Invasive cystoscopy is not indicated for uncomplicated asymptomatic bacteriuria and carries unnecessary instrumentation risks in pregnancy.

subject: Medicine
topic: Sexually Transmitted Cervicitis and Urethritis Updated CDC Therapy Guidelines
stem: A 23-year-old man presents to an urgent care clinic with a 3-day history of burning with urination and a profuse, yellowish-green, purulent urethral discharge. He reports having unprotected receptive and insertive sexual intercourse with a new male partner 6 days ago. Physical examination demonstrates an uncircumcised penis with spontaneous purulent discharge exuding from the urethral meatus; there are no penile ulcers, vesicles, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. A point-of-care urethral swab Gram stain reveals abundant polymorphonuclear neutrophils with numerous intracellular Gram-negative diplococci. A first-catch urine specimen is sent for Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAAT) for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. The patient weighs 78 kg. Which of the following represents the most appropriate, guideline-adherent initial pharmacotherapeutic regimen for this patient according to updated CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections treatment guidelines?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose plus oral azithromycin 1 g single dose
options.explanation: Fluoroquinolones have widespread resistance (>30%) and are contraindicated for empiric gonorrhea; azithromycin is no longer first-line for chlamydia.

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 250 mg single dose combined with oral azithromycin 1 g single dose
options.explanation: This is the obsolete historical regimen; ceftriaxone is now 500 mg IM, and doxycycline 100 mg BID x 7 days has replaced azithromycin.

options.text: Oral cefixime 400 mg single dose monotherapy with no coverage for Chlamydia trachomatis
options.explanation: Oral cefixime achieves lower serum bactericidal levels than ceftriaxone and has higher failure rates; omitting chlamydial coverage is inappropriate.

options.text: Intramuscular ceftriaxone 500 mg single dose plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
options.explanation: This patient presents with acute gonococcal urethritis, confirmed on urethral Gram stain by abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes containing intracellular Gram-negative diplococci (the classic diagnostic appearance of Neisseria gonorrhoeae). To master updated CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI) Treatment Guidelines on USMLE Step 2 CK, the clinician must understand the major guideline updates: (1) UPDATED GONORRHEA TREATMENT: The recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhea is a SINGLE INTRAMUSCULAR DOSE OF CEFTRIAXONE 500 MG IM (for persons weighing < 150 kg; if weight is >= 150 kg, the dose is increased to 1,000 mg IM). The historical dose of 250 mg IM was doubled due to the global emergence of gonococcal strains with elevated minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) to cephalosporins. (2) UPDATED CHLAMYDIA TREATMENT AND CO-INFECTION COVERAGE: Co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis occurs in 10% to 40% of patients with gonorrhea. When chlamydial infection has not been definitively excluded (as in this patient whose NAAT results are pending), treatment must include concurrent coverage for Chlamydia. THE FIRST-LINE REGIMEN FOR CHLAMYDIA TRACHOMATIS IS NOW ORAL DOXYCYCLINE 100 MG TWICE DAILY FOR 7 DAYS. (3) REASON AZITHROMYCIN WAS REPLACED: Historically, oral azithromycin 1 g as a single dose was widely prescribed for chlamydia. However, recent large randomized clinical trials demonstrated that azithromycin has significantly lower microbiological cure rates than doxycycline, particularly for rectal chlamydial infections (cure rates ~75% for azithromycin vs >95% for doxycycline). Furthermore, widespread single-dose azithromycin use has fueled rapid, widespread macrolide resistance in Mycoplasma genitalium (up to 70% resistant) and increasing cephalosporin MICs in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Consequently, azithromycin 1 g is now relegated to an alternative second-line regimen reserved strictly for situations where doxycycline is contraindicated (such as severe tetracycline allergy or pregnancy). (4) MANAGEMENT OF PARTNERS: All sexual partners from the preceding 60 days must be evaluated and treated presumptively with the same regimen. The patient and partner must abstain from sexual intercourse until 7 days after completing therapy and until symptoms resolve.

options.text: Intravenous penicillin G aqueous 24 million units daily for 10 days plus oral metronidazole
options.explanation: Penicillin is useless against gonorrhea due to widespread plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase production; metronidazole does not treat chlamydia.
